title: Exchanging commits: push, fetch, pull
objective: By the end of this lesson you can send and receive work reliably, and you know what to do when a push is rejected — which is the single most common moment of confusion in shared Git use.

blocks.text: Three commands move commits between your copy and the shared one. They are simple individually; the useful understanding is what each does to your working state, and why one of them regularly refuses.

rows: No, but it changes what everyone else sees

blocks.caption: The first push and every push after
lines: git push -u origin feature/upload   # first time: create it on the server and link them
git push                            # afterwards: the link is remembered
git push origin --delete old-branch # remove a branch from the server
git push --tags                     # send tags (they do not travel automatically)

blocks.title: What -u does
blocks.text: It sets the upstream: it records which remote branch your local branch corresponds to. After that, git push and git pull with no arguments know where to go, and git status can tell you how far ahead or behind you are.

blocks.caption: What it looks like
lines: $ git push
! [rejected]        main -> main (fetch first)
error: failed to push some refs
hint: Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do
hint: not have locally.

blocks.text: This is Git protecting someone else's commits. The server has work you have never seen; accepting your push as-is would leave it behind. The fix is to bring their work into yours first, then push the combined result.

blocks.caption: The correct response
lines: git pull                # fetch their work and integrate it into yours
# resolve conflicts if any
git push                # now the server can move forward cleanly
# NEVER the reflex response:
git push --force        # this deletes their commits from the server

blocks.title: --force is how other people's work disappears
blocks.text: Forcing tells the server to replace its branch with yours, discarding whatever it had that you did not. On a shared branch that is data loss for your colleagues. If you genuinely need to overwrite — after rebasing your own feature branch — use --force-with-lease, which refuses when the remote has moved since you last looked.
Pull is two operations, and you get to choose the second

blocks.caption: Merge or rebase on arrival
lines: git pull --no-rebase           # fetch, then explicitly merge
git pull --rebase              # fetch, then replay your commits on top
git config --global pull.rebase true   # make rebase the default for you

blocks.text: Plain pull creates a merge commit whenever both sides moved, which produces a history full of 'Merge branch main of ...' entries that say nothing. Pull with rebase replays your local commits on top of theirs and keeps the line straight. Since your unpushed commits are unshared by definition, rebasing them is safe — this is the one place rebase-by-default is a reasonable choice.

blocks.caption: Where am I relative to the server
lines: git fetch
git status
#   Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 2 commits.     ← you have unpushed work
#   Your branch is behind 'origin/main' by 5 commits.       ← you need to pull
#   Your branch and 'origin/main' have diverged             ← both moved; integrate
git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD    # exactly what you would push
git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main    # exactly what you would receive

blocks.title: Fetch before you judge
blocks.text: Ahead and behind are measured against your last-known note of the server, not the server itself. A status that says 'up to date' can be an hour out of date. Fetch first, then read it.

blocks.title: Cause a rejection and resolve it properly
steps: Using the two repositories from the previous lesson (~/git-lab and ~/git-lab-clone)
In ~/git-lab-clone: echo 'from the clone' >> notes.txt && git commit -am "Change from the clone" && git push
In ~/git-lab: echo 'from the original' >> notes.txt && git commit -am "Change from the original"
Run: git push                  (rejected — the server has work you do not)
Run: git pull --rebase         (replay your commit on top; resolve the conflict)
blocks.expected: A rejection you caused on purpose, then the correct resolution: pull, integrate, push. The history stays a straight line because you rebased your own unshared commit rather than forcing it over someone else's.

cheatsheet: fetch = download and update notes · pull = fetch + integrate · push = send
git push -u origin <branch> the first time; git push afterwards
A rejected push means the server has commits you do not have
The fix is pull then push — never --force on a shared branch
--force-with-lease is the safe version, and only for your own rebased branch
git pull --rebase keeps history straight; pull.rebase true makes it your default
git log origin/main..HEAD — exactly what you would push
git log HEAD..origin/main — exactly what you would receive
Ahead/behind are measured against your last fetch, so fetch before judging
Tags do not travel with a normal push — use git push --tags

checkpoint.prompt: Your push is rejected with 'the remote contains work that you do not have locally'. What is the correct response?

choices.B: git pull, integrate the other work, then git push
choices.D: Delete your branch and start again

checkpoint.explanation: The rejection exists to protect commits you have not seen. Forcing would remove them from the server, which is data loss for whoever made them.

checkpoint.prompt: What is the difference between fetch and pull?

choices.C: Fetch updates your remote-tracking notes only
choices.D: None; pull is just a shorter alias for the same fetch

checkpoint.explanation: Pull does that and then integrates the work into your branch. Fetch changes what you know. Pull changes what you have — which is why fetch is always safe and pull can produce conflicts. Fetch does download the new commits — but it only ever updates your notes, not your branch.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is git pull --rebase often preferred over plain git pull?

choices.C: It replays your unpushed commits on top of the incoming work
choices.D: It is faster over the network because it downloads less data each time

checkpoint.explanation: Your unpushed commits are unshared, so rebasing them is safe — and it keeps the shared history readable instead of filling it with automatic merges. That is what avoids a history full of uninformative merge commits.

checkpoint.prompt: git status says you are up to date. What should you check first?

choices.C: Whether you are on the right operating system

checkpoint.explanation: Ahead/behind uses local remote-tracking refs rather than a live server view. Fetch and pull update them, and a successful push may update the associated tracking ref too. Run fetch when you need a fresh comparison with other server-side changes.
